steps.en: The right ventricle fails the left ventricle test: it is crescent shaped, wraps around the left, and no single view shows it whole. Assessment therefore combines size in a dedicated right ventricle focused four chamber view with two longitudinal function measures, TAPSE and the S prime tissue velocity. Together they answer whether the right heart is dilated, whether it pumps along its long axis, and whether raised pulmonary pressure or infarction is the likely cause. In India this matters in rheumatic mitral stenosis, where long standing pulmonary venous hypertension dilates and weakens the right heart.
From the apical four chamber, slide medially and rotate slightly until the right ventricle dominates the screen with the apex centred and the free wall fully seen.
Measure basal diameter at the annulus level, mid diameter halfway up, and length from annulus to apex, all at end diastole.
Place M mode through the lateral tricuspid annulus and measure its systolic excursion toward the apex as TAPSE.
Place tissue Doppler on the same annular spot and record the systolic S prime velocity.
Measure free wall thickness from the subcostal view at end diastole, keeping the beam perpendicular.
Read size with TAPSE and S prime together, then look for the cause: septal flattening, pulmonary pressure, or regional wall change.

Measuring the right ventricle in a left centred four chamber. Fix: Slide and rotate until the right ventricle is largest on screen with a centred apex. A standard four chamber underreads the right side.
Including trabeculation in diameters or wall thickness. Fix: Drop the cavity gain and trace compact wall only; trabeculation and the moderator band belong inside the cavity.
Off angle M mode through the annulus. Fix: Align the M mode line with annular motion. An angled line underreads excursion.
Trusting TAPSE alone after right ventricular infarction. Fix: TAPSE follows the base only, so pair it with fractional area change or visual wall reading after infarction.
Right ventricular basal diameter, end diastole. 41 mm or less. Source: ASE 2015 chamber quantification, section on right ventricular size
Right ventricular mid diameter, end diastole. 35 mm or less. Source: ASE 2015 chamber quantification, section on right ventricular size
Tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion. 17 mm or more is normal. Source: ASE 2015 chamber quantification, section on right ventricular systolic function
Tricuspid lateral annular systolic velocity. S prime 9.5 cm per s or more is normal. Source: ASE 2015 chamber quantification, section on right ventricular systolic function
Right ventricular free wall thickness. 5 mm or less at end diastole. Source: ASE 2010 right heart guideline by Rudski and colleagues, section on wall thickness
Severe tricuspid regurgitation can keep TAPSE looking normal while the ventricle fails by volume, so read size with function.
After cardiac surgery the septum moves oddly and TAPSE falls without true failure, so compare with preoperative studies.
Pulmonary pressure estimates need a full tricuspid envelope; a faint trace underreads pressure badly.

q.en: In which view are right ventricular diameters measured?

o.en: Standard left centred apical four chamber
Parasternal short axis at the aortic valve
Right ventricle focused apical view with centred apex

why.en: Diameters belong in the right ventricle focused four chamber, where the right ventricle is largest on screen and the apex is centred.
Normal TAPSE is 17 mm or more, so a value below 17 mm marks longitudinal systolic dysfunction.

q.en: Which tricuspid S prime is normal?

why.en: A lateral annular systolic velocity of 9.5 cm per s or more is the ASE 2015 normality threshold.

q.en: A basal diameter of 45 mm is abnormal in which structure?

why.en: The basal right ventricular diameter limit is 41 mm, so 45 mm means right ventricular dilatation.
